blocks.text: A thermistor is a heat sensitive resistor. Most thermistors have negative temperature coefficient of resistance, i.e., the resistance of such thermistors decreases when their temperature is increased. Thermistors with positive temperature coefficient are also available.

blocks.alt: Two thermistor symbols. Left: a zigzag resistor inside an oval with a diagonal arrow across it pointing up to the left. Right: a rectangle with leads on both sides, crossed by a slanting line that ends in a short horizontal foot at the bottom left.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.33: Thermistor symbols (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.33).

blocks.text: In the thermistors, resistance decreases as temperature increases. This is because increasing temperature provides more energy to the charge carriers (electrons or holes), enabling them to move more freely and thus reducing resistance.

Thermistors are made by heating under high pressure semiconductor ceramic made from mixtures of metallic oxides of manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper, iron, etc. These are pressed into desired shapes and then baked at high temperature. Different types of thermistors are shown in Fig. 9.34. They may be in the form of beads, rods or washers.

blocks.alt: A row of thermistors on a white background, from left: a black disc on two long silver leads; a long thin black rod on a tan lead; a short black rod on two tan leads; a dark brown oval bead; a small black bead with bent leads; a black body with a ring (washer) lug on top; a small grey block; then a large black disc and a large green disc, each on two leads.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.34: Types of thermistors (original drawing after the photograph printed in the textbook's Figure 9.34).
